requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'Equivalence Checking of ML GPU Kernels' have been reproduced: implementing Volta, an equivalence checker for GPU kernels operating on PTX assembly, and reproducing its evaluation on human-generated, LLM-generated, and compiler-generated ML kernels.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware, software dependencies (SymPy, SymEngine, Python/C++ toolchain), CUDA/PTX toolchain (ISA 9.0, nvcc), and GPU environment required to build and run Volta are set up correctly.

System-level toolchain and hardware environment: NVIDIA CUDA toolkit with PTX ISA 9.0 support, nvcc compiler for translating CUDA/CUTLASS to PTX, and a compatible GPU are available for producing and analyzing PTX inputs.

Code has been implemented that installs or configures the NVIDIA CUDA toolkit including nvcc with support for PTX ISA 9.0, and provides a documented invocation (e.g., in a README, Dockerfile, or setup script) to compile CUDA kernels down to PTX using this toolchain.
Code has been implemented that verifies nvcc emits PTX targeting ISA 9.0 (e.g., via '.version 9.0' in the generated PTX header) for the benchmark kernels used by Volta.

Code has been implemented that provides a runnable script or documented procedure to compile CUTLASS-templated kernels (used in Table 5 TileLang and tensor-core benchmarks) to PTX via nvcc, so the resulting PTX can be fed to Volta.

The evaluation harness targets and runs on a machine with a 24-core 2.64 GHz AMD EPYC 7413-class CPU and at least 220 GB of RAM (or documents equivalent hardware), matching the environment used to report Volta's runtimes.
Python-side dependencies for the simulator: a Python interpreter with SymPy installed and configured to represent both symbolic and concrete values uniformly during PTX symbolic execution.

Code has been implemented that pins and installs a specific Python version and SymPy version (via requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, environment.yml, or equivalent) sufficient to run Volta's simulator.

Code has been implemented that imports SymPy and uses SymPy expressions as the uniform representation for both symbolic inputs (fresh symbols for tensor elements) and concrete constants inside the simulator's program state.

The simulator invokes SymPy's built-in simplification for arithmetic used in address computation and branch predicate evaluation, so that array offsets and control-flow predicates reduce to concrete integers/booleans when statically determined.
C++ decision-procedure dependencies: a C++ toolchain and SymEngine are installed and linked so the decision procedure binary can be built and invoked on serialized symbolic expressions.
Code has been implemented that provides a build system (e.g., CMake or Makefile) which compiles the C++ decision procedure sources against SymEngine and produces an executable used by Volta.

Code has been implemented that installs SymEngine (from source or package) with a documented version, and the build succeeds against that SymEngine, replacing the earlier SymPy-based decision procedure prototype.

The C++ decision procedure enables multi-threaded evaluation of verification conditions (each VC checked concurrently) so that per-output-element checks run in parallel, matching the paper's stated 'embarrassingly parallel' implementation.
PTX ingestion infrastructure: Volta accepts PTX ISA 9.0 assembly plus user-provided annotations, and the tooling glues nvcc-produced PTX to the simulator and decision procedure end-to-end.

Code has been implemented that provides a command-line entry point taking two PTX files (reference and optimized) plus an annotation file/flags specifying thread count and input/output tensor arrays, and drives the full pipeline (parse -> simulate -> serialize -> decide).

Code has been implemented that serializes the final symbolic state (G and R) restricted to output-tensor elements into a custom on-disk format, which the C++ decision procedure then loads to construct verification conditions f - g.

The pipeline is verified end-to-end on at least one sanity benchmark (e.g., Red-1 vs Red-1) and completes without environment/toolchain errors, producing an 'equivalent' verdict as reported in Table 1.

Reproducibility of reported runtimes: the environment yields end-to-end equivalence-checking times consistent with the paper's claim that all evaluated benchmarks complete in under 10 minutes on the specified machine.

The formal language L of structured-CTAs, including its syntax, unchecked small-step dynamics (Schd, Sync, Const, BinOp, RdReg, RdMem, WrMem), and checked dynamics with race-tracking context X (RdMem', WrMem', Sync', RdMemBad, WrMemBad, SchdBad) has been implemented.

The syntax of L (Figure 3) is faithfully represented: programs P are parallel compositions of thread programs T; thread programs are sequences of statements terminated by return; statements include register assignment (r := c), binary operation (r := r1 op r2), memory read (r := *g), memory write (*g := r), and sync I for a set of thread IDs I.

Code has been implemented that defines an abstract syntax (data type / class hierarchy) for L programs comprising registers r, constants c, shared-memory addresses g, thread ID sets I, per-thread straight-line statement lists, and sync I markers, matching the grammar in Figure 3.
Code has been implemented so that a top-level program P is represented as an indexed collection of per-thread programs (T_1 || T_2 || ... || T_N), addressable by thread ID i.
Every well-formed thread program T in L must terminate with a return statement, and this invariant is enforced (or checked) by the implementation.

Configurations for the two small-step relations are implemented: top-level configurations (G, R, P) with shared memory G, register-file map R indexed by thread ID, and program P; thread-level configurations (G, R, T) with an additional race-tracking context X for the checked dynamics.
Code has been implemented representing shared memory G as a map from addresses g to values, supporting functional update G[g -> v] as used by RdMem/WrMem rules.
Code has been implemented representing R as a map from thread IDs to per-thread register files (each a map from register name to value), with functional update R[i -> R'].

Code has been implemented for the race-tracking context X: for each address g, X(g) stores (rd, wr) where rd maps each thread i to the set of threads that have not synchronized with i since its last read of g, and wr = (j, J) records the last writer j and threads J that have not synchronized with j since it wrote g.
Code has been implemented for the initial empty context X_empty = lambda _. ((lambda _. empty), (0, empty)) as described in the paper, used as the starting X for symbolic execution.
The unchecked small-step dynamics of L (Schd, Sync, Const, BinOp, RdReg, RdMem, WrMem) are implemented.
Code has been implemented for the Schd rule that non-deterministically selects any thread i not blocked at a sync and advances it via a thread-level step, updating R[i] and P[i] accordingly.

Code has been implemented for the Sync rule advancing all threads blocked at sync I only when every thread in I is currently at sync I or return; if any two blocked threads use incompatible sync sets I1 != I2 with i1,i2 in I1 ∩ I2, the program is stuck (deadlock).
Code has been implemented for the Const (r := c), BinOp (r := r1 op r2 using operator ⊕), and RdReg rules that perform the corresponding functional updates on R and advance the thread program T.
Code has been implemented for the RdMem rule (r := *g reads G(g) into R(r)) and WrMem rule (*g := r writes R(r) into G(g)), matching the transition rules in Section 4.1.

When a thread program has been reduced to return, no thread-level step applies to that thread; the top-level relation still allows Sync involving that thread (return counts as blocked), consistent with PTX early termination.
The checked small-step dynamics with race tracking are implemented: RdMem', WrMem', Sync' update X, and RdMemBad, WrMemBad, SchdBad transition to the error value ⊥ when a race is detected.
Code has been implemented for the predicates noRacingRd(i, rd) := for all j, i = j or i not in rd(j), and noRacingWr(i, (j, J)) := i = j or i not in J, exactly as defined in Section 4.2.

Code has been implemented for RdMem': on a read *g by thread i, when noRacingRd and noRacingWr hold on X(g), it performs the usual read into R(r), updates rd(i) to the full thread set I (recording that i must synchronize with every other thread before another access races), and leaves wr unchanged.

Code has been implemented for WrMem': on a write *g := r by thread i, when noRacingRd and noRacingWr hold on X(g), it writes R(r) to G(g), sets X(g).wr to (i, I \ {i}) marking i as new last writer with all other threads unsynchronized, and resets the read map for g.

Code has been implemented for Sync' that, in addition to advancing threads past sync I, updates X via syncMem(I, X): for each address g, syncMemRd removes threads in I from rd(i) for i in I, and syncMemWr shrinks J by threads in I when the last writer j is in I, exactly as in Section 4.2.

The helper functions syncMemRd(I, rd)(i) = (rd(i) \ I) if i in I else rd(i), syncMemWr(I, (j, J)) = (j, J \ I) if j in I else (j, J), and syncMem(I, X)(g) applying both to the pair X(g), are implemented as separate composable functions.

Code has been implemented for RdMemBad: when executing r := *g under checked dynamics, if noRacingRd(i, rd) is false OR noRacingWr(i, wr) is false for X(g), the whole configuration transitions to the error value ⊥.
Code has been implemented for WrMemBad: when executing *g := r under checked dynamics, if either noRacingRd(i, rd) or noRacingWr(i, wr) fails for X(g), the configuration transitions to ⊥.

Code has been implemented for SchdBad lifting thread-level ⊥ to the top-level configuration: if the thread-level checked step for thread i produces ⊥, then (X, G, R, P) transitions to ⊥ at the top level.
Once the configuration reaches ⊥, no further steps are possible and the reflexive-transitive closure ↩→* preserves ⊥ (i.e., ⊥ is an absorbing terminal state used for race/deadlock reporting).
Deterministic behavioral checks demonstrate that the implemented dynamics correctly detects the canonical race, deadlock, and race-free scenarios described in Section 4.

Running the checked dynamics on the naive-softmax expansion of Figure 2 with the __syncthreads barrier REMOVED yields ⊥ (a data race is reported), while with the barrier present it terminates in all-return without ⊥.

For a program in which one thread executes sync I1 and another executes sync I2 with I1 != I2 and i1, i2 in I1 ∩ I2, the top-level relation gets stuck (no Sync rule applies), as required by the deadlock-conservative treatment in Section 4.1.

After a Sync' step over a set I containing all threads that read/wrote an address g, X(g) is reset so that subsequent reads and writes by threads in I no longer trigger RdMemBad/WrMemBad (verifiable via a small unit test).

The Sync rule fires when every thread in I is at either sync I or return, matching the PTX early-termination semantics — a unit test with one thread already at return and the others at sync I successfully advances.

The implementation enforces the structured-CTA assumptions on inputs: statically-known tensor tile sizes, statically-resolvable branch targets, statically-resolvable memory addresses, and straight-line per-thread bodies after loop unrolling; kernels violating these constraints raise an exception.
Code has been implemented that requires all tensor tile sizes accessed by a CTA to be statically known from user annotations; kernels with unknown sizes cause Volta to raise an exception.

Code has been implemented that resolves conditional branch targets statically per thread (given its tid) and raises an exception if a branch predicate cannot be reduced to a constant during symbolic execution.
Code has been implemented so that every memory access address (base array plus index) simplifies to a statically-known constant per thread; data-dependent addresses cause Volta to raise an exception.

After per-thread specialization (unrolling loops and resolving branches), each thread program is a straight-line list of L statements ending in return, as reflected in the language syntax of Figure 3.

Out-of-bounds reads or writes to statically-sized arrays, and reads from uninitialized registers/memory, cause Volta to raise an exception rather than silently returning zero (as noted in Sections 5 and 6.2).

The PTX parser producing the low-level statement IR and the round-robin symbolic simulator/scheduler (with X, G, R state, queue-based per-thread program counters, exception raising for structured-CTA violations, out-of-bounds accesses, uninitialized reads, deadlocks, and data races) has been implemented as described in Section 5.
The PTX parser consumes PTX ISA 9.0 assembly (with user annotations for thread count and input/output tensors) and lowers each instruction to a statement record used by the simulator.
Code has been implemented that accepts PTX assembly conforming to PTX ISA 9.0 as produced by nvcc and reads the assembly file into an in-memory representation.

Code has been implemented that accepts user-provided annotations specifying the number of threads in the CTA and which arrays are input tensors versus output tensors, and threads/tensors declared in annotations are exposed to the scheduler.
Each parsed PTX instruction is encoded as a statement record containing an opcode, a destination, a list of arguments, and an optional predicate for conditional execution.
The parser supports all PTX opcode families exercised by the paper's benchmarks, including memory loads/stores, arithmetic operations, jumps/branches, and labels.
Predicated PTX instructions parse with their guard predicate attached to the statement record, and the simulator uses that predicate to conditionally execute the statement.
The parser produces an ordered list of statements for a single CTA that is handed to the scheduler as the program shared across all threads.

The simulator maintains program state consisting of X (memory-event context), G (shared memory), and R (per-thread register files) using SymPy expressions to uniformly represent symbolic and concrete values.
Code has been implemented for G, a map from shared-memory addresses to SymPy value expressions, supporting read and write of scalar values at specific addresses.
Code has been implemented for R, a per-thread register file mapping (thread id, register name) to SymPy value expressions.

Code has been implemented for X, tracking for each shared-memory address the set of readers per thread that have not yet synchronized with the current thread, and the last writer along with the set of threads that have not yet synchronized with that writer.
State entries use SymPy expressions uniformly so that both concrete constants and symbolic input-tensor symbols are handled by the same read/write/arithmetic pathways.

For each declared input tensor element the simulator initializes G (or the appropriate memory) with a fresh SymPy symbol, and initializes X to the empty context X_emptyset (no prior readers or writers).
The round-robin scheduler advances threads using a queue of (thread_id, program_counter) pairs sharing one copy of the statement list until all threads reach return.
For a CTA with threads 0..N-1 the scheduler initializes its queue to [(0,0),(1,0),...,(N-1,0)], each pair being (thread_id, program_counter).
All threads share a single copy of the parsed statement list; the scheduler stores only per-thread program counters rather than duplicating the program per thread.

On each iteration the scheduler dequeues one (thread_id, pc) pair, symbolically executes that thread's statements until it blocks (barrier) or returns, updates state, then re-enqueues the updated pc if the thread is not returned.
Round-robin scheduling terminates cleanly once all threads have executed a return instruction, and the final G, R state is exposed to the downstream verification-condition generator.
The scheduler executes each thread's statements in linear time in N (the number of statements per thread), matching the linear-in-N simulator complexity described in Section 5.
Symbolic evaluation of individual PTX statements updates G, R, and X and uses SymPy simplification to evaluate offsets, predicates, and arithmetic.

Arithmetic PTX instructions (add, sub, mul, div, fma, exp, max, etc.) are evaluated by constructing the corresponding SymPy expression from the source operands and storing it in the destination register.

The simulator invokes SymPy's simplification when computing shared-memory addresses and when evaluating branch predicates so that address offsets and predicate truth values reduce to concrete integers/booleans whenever possible.

Conditional and unconditional branches update the thread's program counter based on the (statically resolvable) predicate value; if the predicate does not reduce to a concrete boolean an exception is raised (violation of structured-CTA).
Memory read/write instructions compute the base array and index via SymPy simplification, then read from or write to G at that address, updating X's per-address read/write metadata.
The simulator raises exceptions when input PTX violates structured-CTA assumptions or performs unsafe memory operations, and generates diagnostic reports for deadlocks and data races.
Volta raises an exception when the input PTX is not a structured-CTA, e.g., when a branch target or memory index cannot be statically resolved to a value.
Reading from a register that has not been previously written by the current thread raises an exception rather than producing an arbitrary value.
Reading from a shared-memory location that has not been written raises an exception (uninitialized memory read).

Array reads or writes whose statically-resolved index falls outside the declared bounds raise an out-of-bounds exception, including for shared-memory arrays declared __shared__ (as demonstrated on the 48-element A[tid] example from Section 6.2).
On the Section 6.2 example where 64 threads read from __shared__ int A[48] without guarding tid<48, Volta raises an out-of-bounds exception, while the guarded version passes without exception.

When two threads i1 and i2 synchronize on sets I1 and I2 with I1 != I2 and i1,i2 in I1 intersect I2 (or any configuration that cannot make progress under Sync), the simulator emits a deadlock report and halts.

When the checked dynamics reaches the error state (per RdMemBad/WrMemBad), the simulator generates a data-race report naming the two conflicting accesses (address, thread ids, read/write kind) rather than silently continuing.
The simulator implements bar.sync-style CTA-wide barriers and warp-level barriers (syncwarp, mma.sync) that block a subset I of threads and update X accordingly.
bar.sync (syncthreads) is implemented so that a thread reaching the barrier is blocked until all threads in the CTA also reach a matching bar.sync or return, at which point all are released.
Warp-level barriers (bar.warp.sync, syncwarp with mask, mma.sync) are implemented as a sync on the specified subset I of threads within a warp, blocking those threads until all of I arrive.

When a sync on set I fires, X is updated via syncMem: readers rd(i) for i in I have I subtracted, and last-writer sets (j, J) with j in I have J shrunk to J \ I, matching the Sync' rule of Section 4.2.

Threads that have already executed return are treated as satisfying membership in a barrier set I so that the remaining threads in I can still make progress, matching the PTX early-termination semantics.
Race detection is implemented via the noRacingRd and noRacingWr predicates on X, triggering RdMemBad/WrMemBad when violated.
Code implements noRacingRd(i, rd) as: for every thread j, either j==i or i is not in rd(j); a read by thread i to address g is permitted only if this holds on the current X(g).

Code implements noRacingWr(i, (j,J)) as: i==j or i is not in J; a write by thread i to address g is permitted only if this holds on the current X(g)'s writer field, and additionally requires noRacingRd against prior readers.
On a successful read of address g by thread i, X(g).rd is updated so that i's read is recorded against every other thread j (i.e., rd(j) is extended with i for j != i), per the RdMem' rule.
On a successful write of address g by thread i, X(g).wr is set to (i, I\{i}) and X(g).rd is reset to the empty per-thread map, per the WrMem' rule.

For the Section 2 naive softmax expanded into per-thread programs, if __syncthreads is removed the simulator reports a data race between thread 0's read of buf[1] and thread 1's write to buf[1] (or symmetric variants), matching the example given in Section 2.

After simulation, only the symbolic expressions corresponding to output tensor elements are extracted from G/R and written to disk in a custom serialization format for consumption by the decision procedure.
The serializer writes only the SymPy expressions corresponding to elements of the user-declared output tensors, not the full G/R state.

A custom serialization format (not SymPy's default pickling) is used to write the output expressions, motivated by their potentially large size, and a matching deserializer exists for the decision procedure.

The SymEngine-based C++ decision procedure that canonicalizes f-g via bottom-up AST traversal and rewrite rules (max simplifications, additive inverses, e^a * e^b = e^{a+b}, distribution of multiplication over addition, caching), including support for reals with exponentiation as justified by Theorem 5 / Corollary 6, has been implemented.
The core decision-procedure driver that constructs and canonicalizes f - g in SymEngine has been implemented.
Code has been implemented in C++ using the SymEngine library (not SymPy) to represent and manipulate symbolic expressions used by the decision procedure.

Code has been implemented so that, given a verification condition of the form f = g, the decision procedure constructs the SymEngine expression f - g and reports equality by testing whether this expression canonicalizes to zero.
Code has been implemented that traverses the AST of f - g in a bottom-up manner, applying simplification/rewrite rules to each node exactly once per canonicalization pass.
Code has been implemented that, at each internal AST node with commutative children (e.g., Add, Mul), sorts child nodes using SymEngine's internal ordering to obtain a canonical representation.
For a pair of syntactically distinct but mathematically equal input expressions built only from +, *, and constants, the decision procedure canonicalizes f - g to zero and returns equal.
The suite of algebraic rewrite rules applied during canonicalization has been implemented.
Code implements the rewrite rule max(-infinity, x) = x and applies it during bottom-up traversal.
Code implements the rewrite rule max(x, x) = x (idempotence of max).
Code implements the flattening rule max(max(a, b), c) = max(a, b, c) so that nested max expressions collapse into a single n-ary max.
Code implements the additive-inverse rule E + (-E) = 0, canceling matching subterms and their negations inside additive expressions.
Code implements the exponential-product rule e^a * e^b = e^{a+b}, combining products of exponentials into a single exponential of the sum of exponents.
Code implements distribution of multiplication over addition so that (a + b) * c is expanded, enabling collection of coefficients per monomial term.
After distribution, code collects like monomial terms and their coefficients so that a sum of monomials with zero coefficients simplifies to 0.
For a manually constructed expression e^a * e^b - e^{a+b} the decision procedure returns 0, and for max(max(a,b), max(c,-infinity)) - max(a,b,c) it returns 0.
Support for the Real+Exp fragment justified by Theorem 5 / Corollary 6 has been implemented.
The decision procedure accepts expressions built from the signature (R, +, *, exp) over multivariate real polynomial exponents, matching the class covered by Corollary 6.
Code normalizes expressions of the form sum_i p_i(x) * e^{h_i(x)} by grouping terms sharing identical exponent polynomials h_i and summing their polynomial coefficients p_i.
After grouping by exponent, the procedure decides the whole expression equals 0 iff each polynomial coefficient p_i canonicalizes to 0, as justified by Corollary 6.
Code has been implemented to handle max (and analogous piecewise operators) via case splits, as stated in Section 4.4, so that expressions involving max can be decided within the same procedure.

For the softmax verification identity of the motivating example (equating naive softmax output e^alpha / (e^alpha + e^beta + e^gamma + e^delta) with the online-softmax symbolic output), the decision procedure returns equal.
Caching and parallel evaluation of verification conditions have been implemented.
Code has been implemented that caches canonicalized results of AST subexpressions so that repeated occurrences of the same subterm are not recomputed during a decision run.
Code has been implemented that evaluates verification conditions for distinct output-tensor elements concurrently using multi-threading, as described in Section 5.
Code has been implemented that reads the serialized symbolic expressions for output tensors (produced by the simulator) and constructs one SymEngine verification condition per output tensor element.
Integration with the overall Volta pipeline and reporting has been implemented.

If any verification condition fails to canonicalize to zero, the decision procedure reports an equivalence bug for that output element; if all canonicalize to zero, the two programs are declared equivalent, matching the Section 5 description.

The decision procedure treats floating-point tensor values as elements of the reals (i.e., + and * are associative/commutative/distributive as in R), consistent with the paper's stated modeling choice.

The formal properties of Volta---Confluence (Lemma 1), Data Race Freedom (Theorem 1), True Positives Property (Theorem 2), Soundness (Theorem 3), Completeness (Theorem 4), and the decidability results (Theorem 5, Corollary 6)---are validated in the reproduction (e.g., via re-checking the Agda mechanization or spot-checking predictions such as detecting all constructed races and rejecting all constructed non-equivalences).

The checked small-step dynamics (RdMem', WrMem', Sync', RdMemBad, WrMemBad, SchdBad) that instrument the unchecked semantics with the memory-event context X to catch races is implemented and behaves as specified.

Code has been implemented for the memory-event context X mapping each shared address g to a pair (rd, wr) where rd maps a thread i to the set of threads that have not synced with i since its last read of g, and wr is the pair (j, J) tracking the last writer j and threads J that have not synced with j since the write.

Code has been implemented for the predicates noRacingRd(i, rd) := forall j. i=j or i not-in rd(j) and noRacingWr(i, (j, J)) := i=j or i not-in J, and these predicates are used to gate RdMem' and WrMem' transitions.

Sync' updates X via syncMem: for each g, threads in the barrier set I have their read-set entries filtered to remove I, and the writer's non-synced set J is reduced by I when the writer j is in I; leaves other entries unchanged.

RdMemBad and WrMemBad fire (producing bottom) exactly when noRacingRd or noRacingWr fails for the accessing thread on address g, and SchdBad lifts a thread-level bottom to the top-level configuration.

The Agda mechanization of Lemma 1 (Confluence) for the checked small-step relation is reproduced and typechecks, establishing that any two checked traces from a common configuration can be extended to meet.
The Agda development containing the formalization of L, the checked dynamics, and the confluence proof typechecks under a documented Agda version with no holes or postulates in the confluence proof.
A one-step diamond/confluence lemma for the reflexive closure of the checked relation is proven in Agda, from which the many-step confluence (Lemma 1) is derived by tiling.
The commutativity lemma showing that Sync' for I followed by Sync' for J yields the same configuration as Sync' for J followed by Sync' for I (given the hypotheses for both steps) is proven in Agda.

Lemma 1 is stated in Agda exactly as: for all X, G, R, P, if (X,G,R,P) reduces in the reflexive-transitive checked relation to two configurations (X1,G1,R1,P1) and (X2,G2,R2,P2), then there exists (X',G',R',P') reachable from both.
Theorem 1 (Data Race Freedom) and Theorem 2 (True Positives Property) are validated, showing that the checked dynamics detects every real data race and reports no spurious races.

Supporting Lemmas 2, 3, and 4 (unchecked-to-checked simulation up to bottom; checked-to-unchecked reflection; race-detection independence from initial G/R) are proven (in Agda or by mechanized argument) and used in the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2.

Theorem 1 is proven: if program P has a data race under the unchecked dynamics (Brookes-style definition where two conflicting accesses, at least one a write, can directly follow each other in either order), then (X_empty, G, R, P) reduces to bottom under the checked dynamics.

Theorem 2 is proven: if (X_empty, G, R, P) reduces to bottom under the checked dynamics, then P has a concrete data race, i.e., there exist two unchecked traces exhibiting the two conflicting orderings of the racing accesses.

On a suite of hand-constructed racy kernels (e.g., Figure 2 with syncthreads removed, and the Red-5/Red-6/Red-7 warp-synchronous reductions), Volta's symbolic execution flags every constructed data race and produces a diagnostic report.

On the FaialAA canonical false-positive pattern (M[tid]=tid; x=M[tid]; M[x]=...) and on race-free variants of the kernels above, Volta reports no data race, confirming absence of false positives in these constructed cases.

Theorem 3 (Soundness) and Theorem 4 (Completeness) of equivalence checking are validated, tying symbolic execution outputs and the decision procedure Eq to real-valued equivalence of the unchecked programs.
Lemma 5 is proven: for any map phi: (V,oplus) -> (R,oplus), if (G,R,P) reduces under the unchecked dynamics to (G',R',P'), then (phi(G),phi(R),P) reduces to (phi(G'),phi(R'),P').
Lemma 6 is proven using confluence: if (G,R,P) terminates in (G1,R1) and (G2,R2), then either (G1,R1) = (G2,R2) or (X,G,R,P) reduces to bottom for every X.

Theorem 3 is proven: whenever the checked dynamics on symbolic inputs yields (G_P,R_P) for P and (G_Q,R_Q) for Q with Eq(G_P,G_Q) and Eq(R_P,R_Q), and the unchecked dynamics on phi-instantiated inputs terminates for both, the resulting concrete outputs coincide.

Theorem 4 is proven: whenever Eq disagrees on the checked outputs of P and Q on symbolic inputs, there exists a map phi such that the unchecked evaluations on phi-instantiated inputs yield unequal concrete outputs.

Volta rejects a suite of deliberately non-equivalent kernel pairs (e.g., softmax with a missing clipping step, matmul with a wrong accumulation order that is not real-equal, or a modified FA1 kernel with a corrupted update), demonstrating completeness on constructed inequivalences.

The decidability results Theorem 5 (univariate real-polynomial-exponential identities) and Corollary 6 (multivariate extension via random linear substitution and Schwartz-Zippel) are validated and their proofs mechanized or spot-checked to justify Eq's correctness.
Theorem 5 is proven: if p_1(x),...,p_m(x) and pairwise-distinct h_1(x),...,h_m(x) are real polynomials satisfying sum_i p_i(x) e^{h_i(x)} = 0, then every p_i(x) = 0.

Corollary 6 is proven by reducing the multivariate case to Theorem 5 via the random substitution x_i = alpha_i * y and Schwartz-Zippel, showing that pairwise-distinct multivariate h_i preserve distinctness after substitution almost surely.

The claim that for any distinct symbolic terms a, b in V there exists a map phi: (V,+,*,exp) -> (R,+,*,exp) with phi(a) != phi(b) is proven as a corollary of Theorem 5/Corollary 6 and used in the proof of Theorem 4.

The naive softmax and online (FlashAttention-style) softmax kernels of Figure 1 are implemented, Volta produces the expected symbolic outputs for each, and the decision procedure validates their equivalence; missing __syncthreads() is detected as a data race as described in Section 2.
The two softmax reference kernels of Figure 1 are provided as CUDA source and compiled to PTX so Volta can consume them.

Code has been implemented for the naive softmax CUDA kernel of Figure 1(a) which allocates a shared-memory buffer `buf`, has each thread `tid` write `expf(x[tid])` into `buf[tid]`, calls `__syncthreads()`, then has each thread sum `buf[0..N-1]` into `sum` and write `y[tid] = buf[tid] / sum`, specialized to N=4 threads.

Code has been implemented for the online (FlashAttention-style) softmax kernel of Figure 1(b) which maintains running max `m` and denominator `d` over a loop `for (i=0; i<N; i++)` updating `new_m = fmaxf(m, v)`, `d = d * expf(m - new_m) + expf(v - new_m)`, `m = new_m`, and finally writes `y[tid] = expf(x[tid] - m) / d`, specialized to N=4 threads.
Both softmax kernels are compiled with nvcc to PTX (ISA 9.0) files that Volta can parse, and any required user annotations (thread count N=4, input tensor `x`, output tensor `y`) are supplied.
Volta's symbolic execution produces the expected per-thread output expressions for both softmax kernels of Figure 1.
Volta's symbolic evaluator initializes the input environment for the softmax kernel with fresh symbolic values (e.g., x[0]:=α, x[1]:=β, x[2]:=γ, x[3]:=δ) as described in Section 4.

For the naive softmax with __syncthreads() present, Volta's symbolic simulator produces output y[i] = e^{x_i} / (e^{x_0} + e^{x_1} + e^{x_2} + e^{x_3}) for each of the four threads (matching the y_naive expression in Section 2).

For the online softmax (Figure 1b), Volta's symbolic simulator produces output y[tid] = e^{x[tid] - m_N} / d_N where m_N and d_N are the running max and denominator symbolic expressions defined in Section 2.

Round-robin scheduling of the expanded per-thread programs (Figure 2) is implemented so that each column is advanced until it blocks at __syncthreads(), then the next thread is scheduled, matching the description in Section 2.
Volta's decision procedure validates the equivalence identities between the naive and online softmax symbolic outputs.
The decision problem y_naive[i] == e^{x_i - m_N} / d_N is constructed for each i in {0,1,2,3} from the symbolic outputs of the two softmax kernels.
Volta's decision procedure successfully proves all four per-output-element identities between the naive softmax and online softmax symbolic outputs (validating the identities listed in Section 2).
Volta concludes and reports that the naive softmax kernel of Figure 1(a) and the online softmax kernel of Figure 1(b) are semantically equivalent over the reals for all schedules.
Volta detects the missing-__syncthreads() variant of the naive softmax as a data race with the specific diagnostic described in Section 2.

A variant of the naive softmax kernel from Figure 1(a) is created in which the __syncthreads() barrier between the shared-memory write and the sum loop is removed, and compiled to PTX for Volta to analyze.
When run on the no-sync variant, Volta halts with a data-race error (produces ⊥) rather than a normal symbolic output state.

Volta's race diagnostic on the no-sync softmax names a concrete conflicting access pair between threads (e.g., a read of buf[1] by tid=0 racing with the write to buf[1] by tid=1), matching the example given in Section 2.
